Also covers rendering the Ashby job list directly (no CMS) when asked how to show open positions. --- # Wire the Ashby job-board block into the page builder The Ashby integration ships an agnostic core plus an optional Sanity adapter (`lib/integrations/ashby/sanity/`). The adapter is **not** auto-registered into the page builder (that wiring couples to each project's schema), so do it here by editing the project's real files. Read each file first and adapt to its actual shape — do not blindly pattern-match. If an anchor below is missing, stop and report it rather than guessing. ## 0. Preconditions - `lib/integrations/ashby/` exists (the integration was added). - `lib/integrations/ashby/sanity/job-board-block.ts` exists (Sanity adapter — only copied when Sanity is present). If it's missing, the project isn't a Sanity project; skip to **Direct rendering** below. - The project has a page builder: `lib/integrations/sanity/page-builder-config.ts` exists. If not, it's the standard Sanity integration (no page builder) — skip to **Direct rendering**. - Read the `page-builder-block` skill first. Blocks in this template are defined with `defineBlock` and drawn through a registry, and both halves are enforced by a typecheck; the steps below are the Ashby-specific version of that recipe. - `ASHBY_JOB_BOARD_NAME` is set (the slug in the board's `jobs.ashbyhq.com` URL), or the editor will set a per-block `boardName`. No token is needed — Ashby's job-board endpoint is public. `isAshbyConfigured()` from `@/lib/integrations/check-integration` reports whether the env var resolves. ## 1. Re-wrap it with `defineBlock`, then register the schema The shipped adapter uses plain `defineType` so it also works in the standard Sanity integration, which has no page builder. In this template every block must go through `defineBlock` (`lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/shared/block.ts`) — it implies `type: "object"` and appends **Anchor ID** and **Presentation Mode**, the two fields the renderer reads for the anchor and the spacing. Create `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/components/reusable/ashby-job-board.ts` that re-declares the adapter through the factory. Keep the adapter as the source of the fields, so an integration update still flows through: ```ts import { defineBlock } from "@/lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/shared/block" import { ashbyJobBoardBlock as base } from "@/lib/integrations/ashby/sanity/job-board-block" import { jobBoardIcon } from "@/lib/integrations/sanity/icons" export const ashbyJobBoardBlock = defineBlock({ name: base.name, title: base.title, icon: jobBoardIcon, description: base.description, fields: base.fields, preview: base.preview, }) ``` `heading` is one of the fields `resolveAnchorId` walks, so the block gets a generated anchor from the editor's heading with no extra work. Export it from `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/components/index.ts` and add it to the `schema.types` array in `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/index.ts`, alongside the other block types (near `hero` / `description`): ```ts import { ashbyJobBoardBlock } from "./components" // ... export const schema: { types: SchemaTypeDefinition[] } = { types: [ // ...existing component types... ashbyJobBoardBlock, ], } ``` ## 2. Add it to the page-builder config — `lib/integrations/sanity/page-builder-config.ts` Extend the `PageBuilderDocumentType` union and add a block member. Blocks are inlined, so the member is identified by its schema type alone — there is no separate member name and no reference type. Match the member shape the file actually uses — in the current basement page builder that's `pageTypes` (which page documents may host it) plus `category` (which insert-menu group it lands in): ```ts export type PageBuilderDocumentType = | "hero" | "description" | "ashbyJobBoardBlock" // ...rest... // inside pageBuilderBlockMembers: { documentType: "ashbyJobBoardBlock", title: "Job Board", pageTypes: ["generic"], category: "list", }, ``` ## 3. Give it a fixture — `components/page-builder/library.ts` A block's preview is a fixture rendered by the production renderer, not an image: the same entry drives the live pane in the insert menu, the block's row in Studio → **Components** and the `/components` route. # Building scalable CMS components

A project-agnostic guide to building page-builder components on a headless CMS
(Sanity, Contentful, Payload, Storyblok…) with a component framework (React,
Vue, Svelte…). The examples use Sanity + React; the principles don't depend on
either.

> **Agents: never add comments.** When building a component, a schema or a
> variant, write no code comments — no JSDoc, no section banners, no
> explanations of what the code does or why. When working through the Figma
> MCP, add no Figma comments, annotations, sticky notes or explanatory text
> layers. Put explanations in your reply to the user, nowhere else.

## 1. The core idea: content, frame, component

Every page is an ordered list of **blocks**. Each block is three layers, and
each layer owns one thing:

```
Page document
  └─ blocks[]                 ← content: what to say (CMS schema)
       └─ Renderer
            └─ Section frame  ← layout: spacing, width, anchor, rules, surface
                 └─ Container ← max width + side gutters
                      └─ Block component ← draws the content, nothing else
```

- **Schema** describes content, never layout. No pixel fields, no "margin"
  fields, no width toggles per instance.
- **Frame** (one shared `Section` component) owns vertical spacing, width,
  anchor id, section dividers and background surface. It is the same for every
  block.
- **Component** returns content only. It never sets its own outer padding,
  margin or max width.

When a new block is added, spacing, width, anchors and dividers come for free
and are consistent with every other block. That's what scales.

## 2. Anatomy of a block

A block touches a small, fixed set of places. Keep that set explicit and make
the type checker fail when one is missing.

| Piece | Purpose | Make it enforced by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schema | Fields editors fill in | A block factory (below) |
| Insert-menu entry | Category + which page types may host it | Typed config |
| Component | Draws the content | Typed props from generated types |
| Registry entry | Maps block type → component + frame options | Type: exactly one entry per block type |
| Fixture | Sample content used for previews and the component library | Typed against the query result |
| Text/markdown output (optional) | Feeds search, RSS, LLM/crawler mirrors | Type: one renderer per block type |
| Generated types | Schema → TypeScript | CI fails on stale types |

Prefer a **registry object keyed by block type** over a `switch`. With a mapped
type (`{ [T in BlockType]: Entry<T> }`) a missing or extra entry is a compile
error, and each entry receives its block already narrowed to its own type.

## 3. Schema rules

### Use a block factory
Wrap the CMS's type helper in a project helper (`defineBlock`) that every block
must use. It adds the fields every block needs and nothing else:

- **Anchor id** — optional; when empty, derived from the block's title field
  and de-duplicated per page. A hand-typed id always wins.
- **Presentation** — spacing top/bottom (a *step key*, see §5) and optional
  divider toggles.
- When the block declares field groups, put these under a "Presentation" tab
  automatically.

One factory means one place to change behaviour for every block.

### Conventions that pay off
- **Standard field names.** Title fields are always one of a short list
  (`heading`, `headline`, `title`…). Anchors, previews, search and markdown
  output can then read any block generically.
- **Shared field factories** for recurring shapes: section heading (title +
  subtitle + supporting text + CTAs), CTA list (with a max), media, rich text
  with a restricted mark set, background/gradient picker. Never hand-roll a
  second "title + subtitle" pair.
- **Constrain inputs.** Max items on arrays (e.g. two CTAs), restricted rich
  text (bold/italic only where layout can't take more), select lists over free
  text, required where the design breaks without it.
- **Preview title = the block's static name**; identifying content goes in the
  subtitle. Editors scanning a long list need to know *what* each item is.
- **Don't pre-select a field group.** Let editors see all fields first.
- **Two separate axes for availability:** *category* (what the block is —
  hero, text, grid, media…; drives the insert menu) and *page types* (where it
  may be used; drives validation). Collapsing them produces a flat, unusable
  menu.
- **Folder rule:** everything under the "blocks" schema folder is a block;
  shared object types live in a `shared` folder.

### Inline vs reference vs document
| Content is… | Model it as |
| --- | --- |
| Used only on the page that holds it | **Inline object** in the page's block array |
| Shared on purpose (a global footer CTA, a reusable callout) | A **document**, referenced from the block, resolved in the query |
| A collection with its own URL (blog posts, case studies, integrations) | Its **own document type and route**, never a generic page + block |

Inline is the default: no extra lookup per read, no orphaned documents, one id
to address.

### Queries
- Spread block fields (`...`) so new fields flow through without query edits;
  dereference references explicitly.
- Regenerate types after every schema or query change and commit them with the
  change.

### Localisation
Decide per document type whether it's translatable and wire it in one place (a
shared set of language fields + an allow-list of types). Blocks inherit
translation from their page; don't translate per block.

## 4. Component rules

- **Props are the generated query type**, narrowed to the block
  (`Extract<Block, { _type: "banner" }>`). Never hand-write content types.
- **No outer padding, margin or max width on the root.** Internal gaps
  (`gap`, a narrower text column) are fine.
- **Declare emptiness, don't return null.** The registry entry gets an
  `isEmpty(block)`; the renderer skips the block *and* its frame, so an
  unfilled block leaves no empty padded gap and claims no anchor.
- **Clean CMS strings before comparing.** Visual-editing tools (e.g. Sanity
  stega) inject invisible characters into strings; compare `clean(value)`, not
  the raw value.
- **Server-first.** Fetch on the server; mark only the interactive leaf as a
  client component.
- **Frame options live in the registry, in code** — not as editor fields. A
  minimal registry entry has only `render` and `isEmpty`, and a minimal frame
  takes only the anchor id, presentation and a class name. The options below
  are extensions: when the first block needs one, add it to the shared
  registry entry type and to `Section` so every block can use it, instead of
  working around the frame inside a block. Check which ones the project
  already supports before using them.

  | Extension | Use |
  | --- | --- |
  | `width` | `content` (default) · `wide` · `bleed` (full width; the block re-adds `Container` inside) |
  | `flushTop` / `flushBottom` | Drop frame padding (static or per-instance function) |
  | `overlapsNavbar` | First block slides under a transparent header |
  | `className` / `surface` | Background applied to the frame so it covers the padding too |

  Width is a property of the design of the block, not of the instance.

## 5. The spacing scale

### Why
Editors need to adjust rhythm between sections, but only within a designed
scale. So the instance stores a **step key**, never a pixel value, and the
scale itself is a token set.

### How to build one
1. **Define steps as tokens.** Each step: `key`, `name`, value per breakpoint,
   and exactly one `default`. A typical set:

   | Step | Mobile | Tablet | Desktop |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | XS | 12 | 14 | 16 |
   | SM | 16 | 20 | 24 |
   | **MD (default)** | 24 | 28 | 32 |
   | LG | 32 | 40 | 48 |
   | XL | 48 | 64 | 80 |
   | 2XL | 64 | 96 | 128 |

   Use the project's breakpoints; missing smaller values fall back to the
   larger one.
2. **Decide who owns the values.** Either code tokens (simplest) or a CMS
   singleton (editors can tune values without a deploy). If CMS-owned, ship
   identical defaults in code so an empty document renders the same.
3. **Store only the key** on each block (`paddingTop: "lg"`).
4. **Emit CSS custom properties once**, at layout level:
   `--section-space-<key>` per step + `--section-space-default`, redeclared
   inside each breakpoint media query.
5. **The frame resolves with a fallback chain:**
   `var(--section-space-<key>, var(--section-space-default, 2.5rem))`.
6. **Validate** in the schema (one default, unique names, bounded integers), and
   keep the resolver's normalisation, fallbacks and default selection in one place.

### Why it works
- One value change updates every block using that step — no per-block code.
- Responsiveness lives in one stylesheet, not in each component.
- A deleted or unknown key degrades to the default, then to a literal; content
  can't break layout.
- A step with all zeros doubles as "flush".

Horizontal spacing is a separate system: the container's gutter and max widths
as tokens (`--container-gutter`, `--container-content`, `--container-wide`).

## 6. Variants

There are two kinds. Keep them apart.

### Content variants — chosen by editors
A layout/variant field in the schema:

```ts
export const heroVariants = [
  { title: "Band graphic", value: "band" },
  { title: "Full gradient", value: "gradient" },
  { title: "Text only", value: "text" },
] as const

defineField({
  name: "variant", title: "Layout", type: "string",
  options: { list: [...heroVariants], layout: "radio" },
  initialValue: "band",
})
```

- Export the option list once (`as const`); schema, component and fixtures
  share it.
- **Hide fields a variant doesn't use** and make fields **conditionally
  required** per variant. Editors only see what the current layout renders.
- The component dispatches to **one sub-component per variant** in the block's
  folder (`hero/band.tsx`, `hero/gradient.tsx`, shared `types.ts`).
- Variant-dependent frame behaviour (flush, dark header) is a function in the
  registry entry, once the frame supports that option (§4).
- Every variant gets a fixture so it's previewable.

Rule of thumb: a new **layout of the same content** is a variant; **different
content** is a new block.

### Style variants — chosen in code
Use a variant utility (`cva`, `tailwind-variants`, Stitches, vanilla-extract
recipes…):

```ts
const button = cva("inline-flex items-center rounded-sm", {
  variants: {
    variant: { primary: "…", outline: "…", ghost: "…" },
    size: { sm: "…", md: "…" },
    surface: { light: "", dark: "" },
  },
  compoundVariants: [{ variant: "primary", surface: "dark", class: "…" }],
  defaultVariants: { variant: "primary", size: "md", surface: "light" },
})
```

- One axis per concern; combinations via compound variants.
- A `surface` axis describes what the component sits on, not its own colour.
- Prefer variant axes over boolean props, and slots/composition over flags.
- Use a class merger that knows your custom tokens so overrides dedupe.

## 7. Design-system guardrails

Encode these as tokens and, where possible, lint rules:

- **Typography:** text styles are tokens that carry size, line height, weight
  and tracking together; never combine one with a separate weight class.
  Headings balance-wrap, body copy pretty-wraps.
- **Dividers:** grid lines and section rules are a shared component with a
  single colour token, not ad-hoc borders. Section-edge rules are a frame
  toggle; a block that draws its own registers ownership so the toggle drives
  the right one.
- **Surfaces:** a dark section declares itself (`data-surface="dark"`) and
  swaps line/selection colours through variables.
- **Motion:** named duration and easing tokens only; prefer CSS; respect
  reduced motion everywhere.
- **Breakpoints:** one scale, consumed through helpers for image `sizes` and
  media queries; no hand-written queries.
- **Full width:** a `bleed` frame option (added to the frame if it doesn't
  exist yet), never `100vw`.
- **Links, media, consent:** one link component, one image component (with
  required `sizes`), trackers behind consent.

## 8. Previews and checks

- **The fixture is the preview.** One sample per block (and per variant),
  typed against the query result, feeding the CMS insert-menu preview, a Studio
  component list and an internal `/components` page.
- **Type checks** catch missing registry/markdown entries and stale fixtures.
- Gate merges on typegen + typecheck + lint + build.

## 9. Checklist for a new block

- [ ] Could this be a variant of an existing block instead?
- [ ] Every field is content; spacing/width/anchor come from the frame.
- [ ] Built with the block factory; title field uses a standard name.
- [ ] Shared shapes come from shared field factories; inputs constrained.
- [ ] Category + page types set; preview title is the static name.
- [ ] Inline unless shared by design; collections get their own type + route.
- [ ] Component typed from generated types; no outer padding/width.
- [ ] `isEmpty` declared; CMS strings cleaned before comparing.
- [ ] Variants: one exported list, irrelevant fields hidden, one sub-component
      each, one fixture each.
- [ ] Style variants via a variant utility, one axis per concern.
- [ ] Only tokens: spacing steps, type styles, motion, breakpoints, colours.
- [ ] Types regenerated; all checks pass.

# Designing CMS components in Figma

A reference for designing sections (blocks) that editors assemble into pages in
a CMS. Every rule here exists so a Figma component maps one-to-one onto a CMS
block that developers can build once and editors can reuse safely.

> **Agents: never add comments.** When building components or variants through
> the Figma MCP, add no Figma comments, annotations, sticky notes or
> explanatory text layers. When building them in code, write no code comments.
> Put explanations in your reply to the user, nowhere else.

## 1. How pages are built

A page is a vertical stack of **sections**. Each section has three layers:

```
Page
  └─ Section            spacing above/below, background, divider lines
       └─ Container      max width + side margins
            └─ Block      the content: title, text, media, buttons…
```

- **The block is the content only.** It has no outer padding and no margin.
- **The section owns the space around it.** Space between sections comes from a
  shared spacing scale, chosen per section by editors.
- **The container owns width.** Blocks sit inside a fixed content width unless
  they are designed to go full width.

In Figma: design the block component **without outer padding**, and place it
inside a "Section" wrapper frame whose top/bottom padding is bound to a spacing
variable. Don't bake section spacing into the block.

## 2. The spacing scale

### What it is
A short list of named steps editors pick from for the space above and below
each section. Editors never type pixel values, so every page stays on rhythm.

| Step | Mobile | Tablet | Desktop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| XS | 12 | 14 | 16 |
| SM | 16 | 20 | 24 |
| **MD (default)** | 24 | 28 | 32 |
| LG | 32 | 40 | 48 |
| XL | 48 | 64 | 80 |
| 2XL | 64 | 96 | 128 |

(Example values — agree yours with developers. One step is always the
default.)

### How to set it up in Figma
1. Create a variable collection, e.g. **Spacing / Section**, with one number
   variable per step (`section/xs` … `section/2xl`).
2. Add **modes** for each breakpoint: Mobile, Tablet, Desktop.
3. Bind the Section wrapper's top and bottom padding to these variables.
4. Switch the page frame's mode to preview every breakpoint at once.

### Why it works
- Change one value and every section using that step updates — in Figma and on
  the site.
- Sizes respond to breakpoints automatically, so you design rhythm once.
- If a section needs space that isn't on the scale, that's a signal: either
  add a step to the scale (for everyone) or the spacing belongs *inside* the
  block.

### Spacing inside a block
Gaps between a block's own parts (title → text → buttons) are part of the
block. Use auto layout gaps bound to your general spacing variables, not
one-off numbers.

## 3. Width and layout

Every block declares one width, by design (editors don't change it):

| Width | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **Content** (default) | Most blocks. Sits in the standard max width with side margins. |
| **Wide** | Extra-wide layouts (large galleries, wide carousels). |
| **Full bleed** | Edge-to-edge backgrounds or media. Inner text still aligns to the content width. |

- Use a shared **layout grid style** per breakpoint (columns, gutter, margin)
  and align every block to it.
- A full-bleed block still aligns its text and buttons to the content
  container, so the page reads as one column.
- Narrower measures *inside* a block (a readable text column) are fine.

## 4. Components and variants

### Block = one Figma component set
Each block is one component set. Its **properties map to CMS fields**, so name
them the way editors will see them.

| Figma property | Becomes in the CMS | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Variant** (`Layout`) | A layout dropdown | Hero → Band · Gradient · Text only |
| **Text** property | A text field | `Title`, `Subtitle`, `Eyebrow` |
| **Boolean** property | An optional field (shown only when filled) | `Show eyebrow`, `Show CTA` |
| **Instance swap** | A choice from a fixed set | Icon, graphic, logo |
| Nested component | A shared field group reused across blocks | Section heading, CTA button |

### Content variants vs new blocks
- **Same content, different arrangement → a variant** (`Layout` property).
- **Different content → a new block.**
- If a variant needs fields the others don't, note it — those fields will be
  hidden for the other layouts in the CMS.

Before adding a block, check whether an existing block plus a new layout
covers it. Fewer, flexible blocks scale better than many single-use ones.

### Style variants (shared UI components)
Buttons, cards, chips, inputs are smaller components with **one property per
concern**:

- `Variant` (Primary / Outline / Ghost), `Size` (S / M), `Surface`
  (Light / Dark), `State` (Default / Hover / Focus / Disabled).
- `Surface` means *what it sits on*, not its own colour — a primary button on a
  dark section is `Surface = Dark`.
- Prefer a property over a duplicated component; prefer a slot (instance swap)
  over a dozen booleans.

### Reuse shared building blocks
Recurring patterns are one nested component everywhere:

- **Section heading** — title + optional subtitle + optional supporting text +
  up to 2 buttons. Don't design a second title/subtitle pair.
- **CTA** — label + link, max 2 per block, from a fixed set of button styles.
- **Background** — picked from a shared library (e.g. gradients), never a
  one-off image per block.

## 5. Designing for real content

Editors will fill these with any content. Design for that, not for the ideal
copy.

- **Every field gets limits.** Note max characters for titles, max items for
  lists, number of buttons. These become CMS validation.
- **Mark required vs optional.** Show the block with only required fields
  filled — that's the minimum state, and it must still look intentional.
- **Show the extremes:** shortest and longest title, 1 item vs max items, no
  image, a 2-line button label.
- **Rich text:** specify which formatting is allowed (often bold and italic
  only).
- **Images:** specify aspect ratio, crop behaviour and what happens on small
  screens. Media always has alt text in the CMS.
- **Empty block:** if the key content is missing, the block disappears from the
  page entirely (including its spacing) — no empty-state design needed unless
  it's a listing (e.g. "no results").
- **Anchor links:** each section can be linked to (`/page#section`); the id
  comes from the block's title. Keep a clear title layer in each block.

## 6. Tokens only

- **Type:** use text styles only; each style already includes its weight — don't
  override weight on an instance. Headings are balanced (even line lengths),
  body copy avoids single-word last lines.
- **Colour:** colour variables only, with light/dark modes. A dark section uses
  the dark mode for text, lines and buttons.
- **Lines and dividers:** a shared Divider/Line component with one colour
  variable, not strokes on frames. Lines at the top/bottom of a section are a
  section setting (on/off), not part of the block — unless the line is
  structural to the block's design; call that out.
- **Spacing:** spacing variables only (section scale + internal gaps).
- **Radius, shadows, effects:** from styles, not custom values.
- **Motion:** use the named durations and easings from the motion spec; note
  the trigger (on load, on scroll, on hover) and the reduced-motion fallback
  (usually a simple fade or no motion).

## 7. Breakpoints

- Design every block at **Mobile, Tablet and Desktop** (and wide desktop if
  the layout changes there), using the project's breakpoint values.
- Use variable modes for spacing and type sizes rather than separate
  hand-tuned frames.
- Note what changes at each breakpoint: column count, stacking order, hidden
  elements, image crop.
- Hover-only interactions need a touch equivalent.

## 8. Naming and file structure

- **Block names** are what editors read in the CMS menu: short, descriptive,
  stable (`Hero`, `Logo Wall`, `Stats`). Don't rename after build without
  telling developers.
- **Group blocks by category:** Hero, Banner, Text, Grid, List, Carousel,
  Media, Form, Content.
- **Property and layer names** match the CMS field names (`Title`, not
  `Text 4`).
- One page per category in the library file; one component set per block;
  every variant and the min/max content states shown next to it.

## 9. Handoff checklist

- [ ] Could this be a new layout of an existing block instead of a new block?
- [ ] Block has no outer padding; section spacing uses the spacing scale.
- [ ] Width is declared: Content, Wide or Full bleed.
- [ ] Properties map to CMS fields and are named like them.
- [ ] Shared parts (section heading, CTA, background) are nested components.
- [ ] Each field: required/optional, character or item limits, allowed
      formatting.
- [ ] Min content, max content and every layout variant shown.
- [ ] Mobile, Tablet and Desktop designed; changes per breakpoint noted.
- [ ] Only text styles, colour variables, spacing variables and effect styles.
- [ ] Light and dark surface versions where the block can sit on both.
- [ ] Motion: token, trigger and reduced-motion fallback noted.
- [ ] Structural dividers called out; other lines left to the section setting.
- [ ] Agents: no Figma comments, annotations or note layers added.

# JSON-LD Structured Data

This project ships typed JSON-LD generators and a `<JsonLd />` component in
`lib/utils/json-ld.tsx`. Never hand-roll a `<script type="application/ld+json">`
tag — import a generator and render it through `<JsonLd />` (it serializes and
escapes `<` for safe embedding).

```tsx
import { JsonLd, generateJobPostingJsonLd } from "@/lib/utils/json-ld"

// inside a server component
{jobs.map((job) => (
  <JsonLd
    key={job.id}
    data={generateJobPostingJsonLd({
      title: job.title,
      description: job.description,
      datePosted: job.publishedAt,
      employmentType: job.type,
      organizationName: job.company,
    })}
  />
))}
```

## Which tier owns the data?

1. **Site-wide identity** (`Organization`, `WebSite`) — already emitted by the
   site layout. Never re-emit these from components or pages. With Sanity,
   editors manage it in Studio → Layout → Structured Data; Company Data social
   links merge into `sameAs` via their "Include in Structured Data" toggle.
2. **Page-level** (Sanity projects only) — editors attach predefined JSON-LD
   blocks (FAQ, Event, Video, Job Posting, Software Application, Item List,
   Custom) to a page under SEO & Metadata → Structured Data (JSON-LD). The
   page document component already renders them. If the content is page-owned
   and editor-managed, point editors to that field instead of coding it.
3. **Component-level** — when a component itself renders structured content
   (from props or CMS data), emit JSON-LD next to the markup using the
   generators below.

## Component → schema mapping

| Component renders                          | Generator                            |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Job / career listings                      | `generateJobPostingJsonLd` (per job) |
| FAQ / accordion Q&A                        | `generateFaqJsonLd`                  |
| Events / agenda                            | `generateEventJsonLd` (per event)    |
| Video player or embed                      | `generateVideoJsonLd`                |
| Curated lists (work, products, post index) | `generateItemListJsonLd`             |
| Article / blog post body                   | `generateArticleJsonLd`              |
| Breadcrumb navigation                      | `generateBreadcrumbJsonLd`           |
| App / tool promo section                   | `generateSoftwareApplicationJsonLd`  |
| Plain marketing pages                      | `generateWebPageJsonLd`              |
| Logo walls, testimonials, generic heroes   | none — don't force structured data   |

## Rules

- Emit from **server components** so the script tags are in the initial HTML.
- One `<JsonLd />` per entity — map each job/event to its own tag instead of
  merging unrelated entities into one block.
- Only emit when the schema's required fields exist (e.g. `JobPosting` needs
  title, description, datePosted). Skip the tag entirely rather than emitting
  partial data.
- Sanity data: run values through `stegaClean` from `next-sanity` before they
  reach JSON-LD (see `components/layout/json-ld` for the pattern), otherwise
  invisible stega characters leak into the emitted markup.
- Don't duplicate: if a page-level Sanity block already covers the content,
  don't also emit it from the component.
- Generators absolutize app-relative URLs (`/jobs/123`) automatically; pass
  absolute URLs (including Sanity CDN assets) as-is.

## Verify

Check `view-source:` for each `application/ld+json` script and validate with
https://validator.schema.org or https://search.google.com/test/rich-results.

name: ketch-consent-check
description: >-
  Gate a tracking or third-party script behind Ketch consent, using the
  project's single consent helper. Use when the user asks to "add
  GTM/PostHog/Claydar/Segment/Hotjar/Clarity", "wire up analytics", "add the
  tracking script", "fire this only with consent", "check consent before
  loading", "make tracking respect consent", "gate this behind cookie consent",
  "stop tracking when someone opts out", or "revoking consent doesn't stop
  tracking". Installing Ketch itself is the `ketch-consent-setup` skill.
---

# Check consent before firing anything

There is exactly one way to ask whether tracking is allowed. Never read
`window.ketch`, `window.semaphore`, cookies or `localStorage` anywhere else —
that is how a codebase ends up with five slightly different, silently wrong
checks and no way to audit them.

Read each file first and adapt to its actual shape — do not blindly
pattern-match. If an anchor below is missing, stop and report it rather than
guessing.

## 0. Preconditions

- `lib/integrations/ketch/` exists. If it doesn't, the consent gate isn't
  installed — stop and run the `ketch-consent-setup` skill first.
- `lib/integrations/ketch/use-consent.ts` exports `useConsent`. If the helper
  has a different shape than below, follow the real file, not this doc.

## 1. Map the tracker to a category

Categories are `essential`, `analytics` and `marketing`. Add the tracker to
`TRACKER_CONSENT_CATEGORY` in `lib/integrations/ketch/categories.ts` so the
mapping lives in one place and is reviewable:

```ts
export const TRACKER_CONSENT_CATEGORY = {
  gtm: "analytics",
  posthog: "analytics",
  claydar: "marketing",
} as const satisfies Record<string, ConsentCategory>
```

How to choose:

| The tracker… | Category |
| --- | --- |
| measures traffic or behaviour (analytics, session replay, heatmaps) | `analytics` |
| builds advertising profiles, retargets, or links identity across sites | `marketing` |
| is required for the site to function (session, security, CSRF) | `essential` |

`essential` is exempt from consent. Do not use it to sneak a tracker through —
if it sends data to a vendor for measurement or advertising, it is not
essential.

When a tool does both (GTM firing ad tags, PostHog with ads integrations
enabled), gate on the **stricter** category, or split it into two loaders.

## 2. Write the loader

```tsx
"use client"

import { useEffect } from "react"
import { useConsent } from "@/lib/integrations/ketch/use-consent"

export const PostHogLoader = () => {
  const { hasConsent } = useConsent()

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!hasConsent("analytics")) return

    const posthog = startPostHog()
    return () => posthog.shutdown()
  }, [hasConsent])

  return null
}
```

Mount it in the same layout as `KetchConsentScript` — the one that renders the
site chrome, typically `app/(content)/layout.tsx`, not the root layout. A
tracker mounted above the CMP would run on admin routes where Ketch never
loads, and `hasConsent` would sit at `false` forever.

Three things make this correct, and all three are load-bearing:

- **`hasConsent` returns `false` until Ketch resolves.** A tracker written this
  way cannot fire before consent. Do not add an "optimistic" path, a timeout
  fallback, or a "load it disabled and enable later" variant.
- **The cleanup function is what makes revocation work.** When the visitor turns
  a category off, `hasConsent` changes, the effect re-runs, and the cleanup
  tears the tracker down — no reload. Without a real cleanup, revoking consent
  silently keeps collecting, which is the actual compliance failure.
- **The dependency is `hasConsent`, not `granted`.** `hasConsent` is stable
  between consent changes, so the effect doesn't thrash.

`useConsent()` also returns `granted`, `isResolved`, `jurisdiction` and
`openPreferences()`.

### If the SDK has no teardown

Some tags can't be unloaded. Then do not load it inside the effect body at all:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  if (!hasConsent("analytics")) return

  let cancelled = false
  const load = async () => {
    const mod = await import("some-sdk")
    if (cancelled) return
    mod.init()
    return mod
  }
  const pending = load()

  return () => {
    cancelled = true
    pending.then((mod) => mod?.optOut())
  }
}, [hasConsent])
```

If there is no `optOut`, no `shutdown`, and no way to stop it, say so
explicitly rather than shipping a gate that only works one way — the vendor may
need to be swapped or fronted by a server-side proxy.

## 3. Scripts outside React

Subscribe to the same store — same default-deny semantics, same live updates:

```ts
import { consentStore } from "@/lib/integrations/ketch/consent-store"

const unsubscribe = consentStore.subscribe(() => {
  if (consentStore.hasConsent("marketing")) startClaydar()
  else stopClaydar()
})
```

`consentStore.hasConsent(category)` reads the current snapshot;
`consentStore.subscribe(fn)` fires on every change and returns an unsubscribe.

## 4. Do not

- **Do not inject the tag unconditionally and "configure consent mode" inside
  it.** The tag must not load at all without consent. A tag that loads and
  self-restricts still opens a connection and often still sets cookies.
- **Do not gate on `isResolved` alone.** That only says Ketch answered, not that
  the visitor said yes.
- **Do not add a second source of truth** (own cookie, a context seeded on the
  server, a `useState` copy). Ketch already persists across navigation and
  reloads; two sources drift and the bug is invisible.
- **Do not read the Ketch purpose code directly** (`"targeted_advertising"`).
  Go through the category names so a purpose rename is a one-line change.
- **Do not gate with `dynamic()` / `next/script` alone.** Deferring a script is
  not consent — it still loads.

## 5. Verify

```bash
bun run typecheck && bun run lint && bun run build
```

Then in the browser, on a page that renders the footer (in a Sanity
page-builder project `/` often 404s and the 404 has no footer — use a real
slug):

1. **Nothing fires before consent.** Fresh profile or cleared storage, open the
   Network tab, filter by the vendor's domain, load the page → zero requests.
   This is the acceptance criterion; check it per tracker, not once.
2. **Accepting starts it.** Accept in the banner → the vendor's request appears
   without a reload.
3. **Revoking stops it.** Open preferences from the footer, turn the category
   off → no further requests, still without a reload. This is what proves the
   cleanup is wired; it is the step most likely to be silently broken.
4. **It survives a reload.** Reload and confirm the choice held, and that the
   tracker's state matches it.

If step 3 passes only after a reload, the effect cleanup is missing or the
tracker was loaded outside the effect. Fix that, don't document it as a
limitation.

## Region note

The helper defaults to denied until Ketch confirms, so trackers stay off even
in opt-out jurisdictions until the consent record arrives. That is stricter
than the law requires and intentional — do not "optimise" it away. The
region-by-region table lives with the project's Ketch documentation.

Steps 2 and 3 of Verify need an explicit Accept/Reject to test, which only
opt-in jurisdictions (EEA/UK, California, Quebec) show. From a default
(notice-only) or opt-out region, consent is auto-granted with no banner
interaction — append `?ketch_jurisdiction=gdpr` to the URL to test the real
gated behaviour instead of assuming it's broken.

  "add the consent gate", "we need cookie consent". Also use for UI questions

  consent widget out of the corner / into the footer", "restyle the consent
  banner", "pass custom styles to Ketch", "make the banner match our design
  tokens", or "why isn't the consent banner showing". Gating an individual

# Install the Ketch consent gate

Ketch is the CMP. It owns the consent record, the jurisdiction resolution, the
legal copy, the banner and preferences modal, and the persistence. The project
owns exactly three things, and this skill wires all three:

1. Loading Ketch's Smart Tag.
2. **One** helper that answers "do I have consent for category X?".
3. An entry point to reopen preferences after the banner is gone.

**Already installed?** If `lib/integrations/ketch/` exists, stop — you want the
`ketch-consent-check` skill instead, which gates an individual tracker.

Read each file first and adapt to its actual shape — do not blindly
pattern-match. If an anchor below is missing, stop and report it rather than
guessing.

## 0. Preconditions

- A basement Next.js project (App Router).
- A Ketch account for the client, with a **property** already created. You need
  its org code and property code. If the property doesn't exist yet, that's a
  dashboard task at https://app.ketch.com and it blocks this skill — report it.
- If you intend to hide Ketch's floating button, a persistent surface every
  template renders — footer, nav, settings menu (in a basement project usually
  `components/layout/footer` reached via `components/layout/wrapper`).

## 1. Env vars

Both codes are public — they appear in the boot URL in the page source — so
they go in as plain values:

```bash
bun run env:set NEXT_PUBLIC_KETCH_ORG_CODE <org_code> --plain
bun run env:set NEXT_PUBLIC_KETCH_PROPERTY_CODE <property_code> --plain
```

Get them from 1Password → **Development** vault → the project's integrations
item. They are the two path segments of the boot URL:

```
https://global.ketchcdn.com/web/v3/config/<org>/<property>/boot.js
```

If all you have is the raw Ketch `<script>` snippet, read both out of that URL.

Because they are plain, **nothing needs to be pushed to Vercel** — the build
reads the committed `.env` and Next inlines them. Do not run
`env:setup-remote` for these.

Document them in `.env.example` too.

## 2. Files — `lib/integrations/ketch/`

Follow the shape of the project's other integrations (e.g.
`lib/integrations/hubspot/`): self-contained folder, relative imports inside it,
`@/` imports across folders, and a `README.md`.

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `env.ts` | Validates both codes against `/^[a-z0-9_-]+$/i`, exports `ketchBootUrl` (`null` when unset) |
| `types.ts` | Types for the `window.ketch` / `window.semaphore` surface |
| `categories.ts` | Category ↔ Ketch purpose ↔ tracker mapping |
| `consent-store.ts` | The only module that talks to Ketch |
| `use-consent.ts` | The helper everything else imports |
| `script.tsx` | Renders the Smart Tag |
| `preferences-button.tsx` | Preferences entry point (`cva`, takes `variant` / `size`) |
| `ketch-experience.css` | Maps Ketch's theme to the project's tokens |

### 2.1 Categories

Three stable local names so nothing else hardcodes a Ketch purpose code:

```ts
export const CONSENT_CATEGORIES = {
  essential: "essential_services",
  analytics: "analytics",
  marketing: "targeted_advertising",
} as const
```

Confirm the right-hand side against the property's real purpose codes:

```bash
curl -s https://global.ketchcdn.com/web/v3/config/<org>/<property>/production/default/en/config.json \
  | jq -r '.purposes[] | "\(.code)  \(.name)"'
```

### 2.2 The store

Module-level state read through `useSyncExternalStore` — no Provider, no
Context. It attaches `ketch('on', 'consent')` and `ketch('on', 'jurisdiction')`
once, on first subscribe, and re-notifies subscribers on every preference
change. `useConsent()` wraps it and exposes `hasConsent(category)`, `granted`,
`isResolved`, `jurisdiction` and `openPreferences()`.

Three facts about Ketch's runtime that the store has to respect:

- Consent arrives as `Record<purposeCode, boolean>`, and a purpose key is
  **absent** until a record exists. **Absent must read as denied** — this is
  what guarantees nothing fires before consent.
- `window.ketch(cmd, …)` pushes onto `window.semaphore`, and Ketch's `boot.js`
  **unshifts** its own `["init", config]` entry. So queuing commands before the
  SDK loads is safe; after init, `semaphore.push` is rebound to dispatch
  directly and `semaphore.loaded` flips to `true`.
- Persistence is Ketch's, not ours: `_ketch_consent_v1_` in `localStorage` plus
  the `_swb` cookie, surviving navigation and reloads. **Do not add a second
  source of truth** — they drift.

### 2.3 knip

Register the folder as an entry or CI fails on "unused exports":

```jsonc
// knip.json
"entry": ["lib/integrations/ketch/**/*.{ts,tsx}", /* …existing… */]
```

## 3. Load the tag

```tsx
export const KetchConsentScript = () => {
  if (!ketchBootUrl) return null
  return <script async src={ketchBootUrl} />
}
```

**Mount it in the layout that renders the site chrome, not the root layout.**
In a basement project that is the route group holding the header and footer —
`app/(content)/layout.tsx` — alongside the entry point from step 4b:

```tsx
const Layout = ({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) => (
  <>
    <KetchConsentScript />
    <Wrapper>{children}</Wrapper>
  </>
)
```

The root layout also wraps admin routes like `/studio`, and a CMP has no
business loading there: nothing on those routes tracks anyone, the banner
covers the tooling, and the floating button lands on top of the Studio UI.
Mounting one level down keeps Ketch on the pages that actually need it.

Two consequences worth knowing, neither of them a problem:

- `script.tsx` imports `ketch-experience.css`, so the styles ride along with
  the component and only ship on the routes that render it. That is what you
  want — it also means the floating-button override is scoped the same way.
- Ketch does not load on the 404, which falls back to the root layout. Fine as
  long as nothing tracks there either. If you later mount a tracker in the root
  layout, move this back up and accept it on `/studio`.

Three traps, all verified on Next 16.3 + React 19:

- **Do not use `next/script` with `strategy="beforeInteractive"`.** It throws
  *"Encountered a script tag while rendering React component"* and emits no
  server-side `<script>`. A plain `<script async src>` is hoisted into `<head>`
  by React 19 during SSR, which is what a CMP needs.
- **Do not render it as a sibling of `<body>`.** A `<script>` as a direct child
  of `<html>` is invalid HTML and produces a cascade of hydration errors. If
  you do mount it in the root layout, it goes *inside* `<body>`.
- **Do not mount it in a layout that some templates skip.** Consent has to be
  askable on every page a visitor can land on. One layout above the footer, not
  per-page.

When `ketchBootUrl` is `null` the tag is not rendered and every consent check
returns `false` — the site degrades to "no tracking", never to "tracking
without consent".

## 4. Decide the UI — do not assume

Ketch ships a banner, a preferences modal and a floating button, all in **light
DOM**, so the project can keep, restyle, reposition or hide any of it. There is
no single correct answer here — **ask, or follow the design.** Do not copy
another project's choice.

Two decisions:

**a. The floating button.** Ketch mounts it into `<div id="lanyard_fab_button">`
as `body.firstChild` whenever the property config has an `accessibilityButton`.

| Option | When |
| --- | --- |
| Keep it as configured | No design opinion yet; fastest path |
| Reposition / restyle it | It collides with a chat widget or sticky CTA |
| Hide it | The design forbids persistent floating UI (common — it covers the layout on every page and is worst on mobile) |

**b. Where preferences are reachable from.** Consent must stay reopenable after
the banner is gone. The floating button, a footer link, a nav item, a
privacy-page link, or several — all valid. If you hide the floating button you
**must** provide another entry point, and it has to be on something every
template renders.

Whatever the project picks, route the call through the integration's helper
(`openPreferences()`), not `window.ketch` directly.

Mechanisms for all of the above — the exact element IDs, why hiding the button
needs `!important`, the available `ketch(…)` commands — are in
[`references/ui-customization.md`](references/ui-customization.md).

## 5. Styling

Ketch's UI is styleable three ways, and they compose. Choose by how much design
control is needed and whether you have dashboard access:

| Approach | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| **Dashboard theme** | Survives code changes, no CSS to maintain — but hexes are duplicated from the design system and drift |
| **`--k-*` variable overrides** | Token-driven, so the design system stays the source of truth and Ketch follows automatically — but the names are Ketch-internal |
| **Direct CSS on Ketch's element IDs** | Total control, needed for layout and responsive work — but couples to Ketch's DOM |

Default recommendation for a basement project: **variables for colour and type,
direct CSS only for structure.** That keeps the banner following the design
tokens with no maintenance, e.g.:

```css
html:root {
  --k-banner-container-background-color: var(--color-primary);
  --k-banner-header-title-color: var(--color-secondary);
  --k-banner-description-link-color: var(--color-contrast);
}
```

Scope overrides to `html:root`, **not** `:root` — Ketch injects its own `:root`
block into `<head>` at runtime, after the project stylesheet.

If there is no design yet, wire it to whatever tokens exist rather than
hardcoding hexes; the UI then updates on its own when real tokens land. Say so
explicitly instead of inventing a visual direction.

Variable naming, how to enumerate what a property exposes, the `!important`
rules, mobile and safe-area handling, and the case for replacing the UI entirely:
[`references/ui-customization.md`](references/ui-customization.md).

## 6. Verify

```bash
bun run typecheck && bun run lint && bun run knip && bun run build
```

Then in the browser:

1. Load a page that renders your chosen entry point. **In a Sanity
   page-builder project `/` is usually a 404** — no page document exists for
   it — and the 404 falls back to the root layout, so it has no chrome and no
   Ketch. Testing there shows no banner and no button and looks broken. Use a
   real slug.
2. The tag is in `<head>`:
   `curl -s <url> | grep -o '<script async[^>]*ketchcdn[^>]*>'`
   If it only appears escaped inside the RSC payload (`\"src\":\"https://…`)
   and not as a real tag, you are looking at a 404, not a page.
3. `window.semaphore.loaded === true` in the console.
4. The banner shows on first visit, and the chosen entry point reopens the
   preferences modal.
5. The floating button is in the state you intended — kept, moved or hidden —
   both while the banner is open and after it's dismissed.
6. Check at <640px too; a widget that looks fine on desktop can cover the
   layout on mobile.
7. Choose something, reload, confirm it persisted.

## 7. Region behaviour — confirm and document it

Ketch resolves a jurisdiction from the visitor's IP and applies that
jurisdiction's legal basis per purpose. This is dashboard configuration, not
code, so **read it rather than assuming**:

```bash
for j in gdpr US_California US_Texas Canada Quebec default; do
  echo "== $j"
  curl -s https://global.ketchcdn.com/web/v3/config/<org>/<property>/production/$j/en/config.json \
    | jq -r '[.regulations[0]] + [.purposes[] | "\(.code)=\(.legalBasisCode)"] | join("  ")'
done
```

Typical result: EEA/UK/CH, California and Quebec are **opt-in**
(`consent_optin` — off until accepted); Canada and most US state-privacy-law
states are **opt-out** (`consent_optout` — on until refused); everywhere else
falls to `default` (`disclosure`, notice only). The full jurisdiction → region
map is in the property's `boot.js` under `jurisdiction.scopes`.

Put the resulting table in the integration's `README.md` — "what an EU visitor
sees vs a US visitor" is a question that gets asked repeatedly.

Note that because the helper defaults to denied until Ketch confirms, the
project's own trackers stay off in opt-out regions too until the record
arrives. That is stricter than required and intentional.

**Opt-out and notice-only jurisdictions won't show Accept/Reject, and the
banner won't come back on reload** once Ketch auto-grants that jurisdiction's
default record — that's the legal basis, not a bug. To actually see and test
the opt-in banner, force a jurisdiction that has one — append
`?ketch_jurisdiction=gdpr` (or `US_Texas`, …) to the URL, no code change
needed. Full mechanics, including a code-level override for previews, are in
`references/ui-customization.md`.

## 8. Document it

Document it wherever the project already documents integrations — a section in
the root `README.md`, or a `lib/integrations/ketch/README.md` if the project uses
per-integration READMEs. Ask rather than adding a file nobody wanted.

Cover: what Ketch is, who owns the account, where the keys live, **how another
integration checks consent before firing**, the region-by-region behaviour, and
open dashboard items.

## Next

Gating an actual tracker (GTM, PostHog, Claydar, …) is the
`ketch-consent-check` skill. Do not wire trackers here.

  agent handles fully, but for a secret the agent only wires the key in code
  (process.env, validation schema, types) and hands the value-setting to the
  human — it never types a secret value into a command. Triggers on "add an env

# Add or change an environment variable

This project uses **dotenvx**. Env files:

- `.env` — shared / development, committed **encrypted**
- `.env.preview`, `.env.production` — per-environment overrides, committed encrypted (created on demand)
- `.env.local` — plaintext, gitignored (personal local overrides)
- `.env.keys` — private keys, gitignored (backed up in the team password manager)

Scripts run `dotenvx run --ignore=MISSING_ENV_FILE -f .env.$VERCEL_ENV -f .env -- …`,
so on Vercel the env-specific file overrides `.env` (locally `VERCEL_ENV` is unset,
so `.env.$VERCEL_ENV` is missing and skipped silently, leaving `.env`). A **gitleaks**
pre-commit hook + CI scan are the real enforcement — this skill just makes the right
choice the default.

## 1. Secret or trivial config?

- **Secret** — API keys, tokens, DB URLs, anything you'd rotate if it leaked.
- **Trivial** — public base URLs, feature flags, anything `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` (it
  ships to the browser anyway). Plaintext is fine; encrypting buys nothing.

## 2a. Secret → never put the value in a command

A raw secret in a command (`env:set KEY <value>`) leaks the plaintext into the
tool call and the conversation context. So split the work:

- **Agent — code wiring only, never the value.** Read it via `process.env.KEY`,
  add it to the env validation schema / types if the project has one, and add a
  placeholder line to `.env.example`. Document the key name and where it's used.
- **Human — owns the value.** Either run `bun run env:set KEY <value>` yourself
  (`--preview` / `--prod` for per-environment), or set it directly in the Vercel
  environment. `env:set` encrypts in place and adds the matching
  `DOTENV_PRIVATE_KEY*` to `.env.keys`.
- **Verify (agent):** only via `git diff` showing `KEY=encrypted:…`. Never run
  `env:view` on a secret — it prints the decrypted value into context.
- Each `DOTENV_PRIVATE_KEY*` must exist on the matching Vercel environment and as a
  CI secret, or it won't decrypt there.
- **Edge runtime caveat.** dotenvx only decrypts in the Node runtime (via
  `instrumentation.ts`). A secret read in `middleware.ts` or a `runtime = "edge"`
  route is **not** decrypted from `.env` — it must be set directly as a Vercel env
  var. The encrypted `.env` covers Node functions + build, not the edge.

## 2b. Trivial config → plaintext

Add it plaintext — no encryption — with `bun run env:set KEY value --plain`, or
just append a line to the file:

```bash
NEXT_PUBLIC_FOO=bar
```

gitleaks ignores non-secret plaintext, so it won't fail the scan.

## Rule

Never commit a real secret in plaintext. If one lands there, bulk-encrypt it in
place with `bun run env:encrypt-all` (no value typed).

  through the renderer's block registry, Anchor ID (generated from the title
  when empty), Presentation Mode, and spacing owned by the frame that instances
  the block rather than the block itself. Use when asked to "add a block to the
  page builder", "create a new section/component for Sanity", "add anchor links
  to a block", "control the spacing of a block from Sanity", or when reviewing

# Page-builder block conventions

Blocks are **inline objects** in the `pageBuilder` array — never documents, and
never referenced. A placement belongs to exactly one page, so the block lives on
that page and nothing is dereferenced at read time. They are drawn by
`components/page-builder/renderer.tsx` through the registry in
`components/page-builder/registry.tsx`. Read one existing block end to end
before writing a new one — `hero` is the smallest complete example:

- schema: `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/components/reusable/hero.ts`
- component: `components/page-builder/components/hero.tsx`
- fixture: `components/page-builder/library.ts`
- registration: `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/components/index.ts`,
  `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/index.ts`,
  `lib/integrations/sanity/page-builder-config.ts`,
  `components/page-builder/registry.tsx`

A block exists in two halves — a schema and a component — and each half has one
place that makes it a block rather than an ordinary object type or a loose React
component. Use them and the conventions below come for free; skip them and a
typecheck fails.

## Non-negotiables

1. **Define the schema with `defineBlock`, never `defineType`.**
   `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/shared/block.ts` implies
   `type: "object"` and appends Anchor ID + Presentation Mode as the last two
   fields. The array member's type name is the block's `_type`, so the schema
   name is also what the registry, the insert menu and the fixture library key
   off:

   ```ts
   import { defineField } from "sanity"
   import { defineBlock } from "@/lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/shared/block"

   export const featureGrid = defineBlock({
     name: "featureGrid",
     title: "Feature Grid",
     icon: featureGridIcon,
     fields: [
       // ...content fields...
     ],
     preview: { /* ... */ },
   })
   ```

   What it adds:
   - `anchorId` — optional. Left empty, the anchor is **generated from the
     block's title** at render time (`resolveAnchorId` in
     `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/shared/anchor.ts` walks `headline`,
     `heading`, `teaserHeading`, `title`, `label` — never `internalTitle`, which
     is Studio-only) and de-duplicated per page. A value typed by hand always
     wins. Name your block's headline field one of those and it works for free.
   - `presentation` — object with `paddingTop` / `paddingBottom`, each storing
     the `_key` of a step from the shared scale. No manual px, ever. A block
     that never touches it follows whichever step is marked as the default.

   Blocks that declare `groups` get a **Presentation** tab for the two fields,
   added automatically — don't list it in `groups` yourself. A block with no
   groups shows them inline, at the bottom of the form.

2. **Register the component in the block registry.** One entry per block, keyed
   by schema type; the renderer has no switch to extend:

   ```tsx
   featureGrid: {
     render: (block) => <FeatureGrid block={block} />,
     isEmpty: (block) => !block.items?.length,
   },
   ```

   - `render` receives the block narrowed to its own `_type`, plus a
     `BlockContext` for page-level values a block doesn't own (`pageId`, the
     blog directory's `listing`). Take the second argument only if you need it.
   - `isEmpty` is optional and declares when the block has nothing to show. The
     renderer then skips the block **and** its `<Section>`, so an unfilled block
     leaves no padded gap behind and doesn't claim an anchor id. Don't
     early-return `null` from the component instead — the renderer has to know
     before it wraps anything.

   The registry's key set is typed as exactly `PageBuilderDocumentType`, so a
   block registered in `page-builder-config.ts` without an entry here — or an
   entry here for a block that was never registered there — is a typecheck
   error.

3. **Never hardcode vertical padding inside a block component.** The renderer
   wraps every block in `<Section>` (`components/page-builder/section.tsx`),
   which renders the `<section>` element, applies the anchor `id` and the
   padding. A block component returns its content only — no outer `<section>`,
   no `py-*` / `pt-*` / `pb-*` on its root. Internal gaps between a block's own
   parts are fine (`gap-*`, `space-y-*`, `mt-*` on children).

   `Section` also lays the block on the page grid (`b-layout-grid`: 4 columns,
   12 from `tablet-lg`, at most 1240px wide). A grid item spans one column by
   default, so the block's root declares its span — `col-span-full`, narrowed
   with `tablet-lg:col-span-*` / `col-start-*` — instead of `max-w-*`,
   `mx-auto` or `px-*`. Nested layouts use `<Grid subgrid>` or a full-width
   `<Grid>` from `components/layout/grid`. Breakpoints are `mobile`, `tablet`,
   `tablet-lg`, `desktop`, `desktop-large` — `sm:`/`md:`/`lg:` compile to
   nothing.

4. **The spacing scale is content, not code.** Editors own it at **Layout →
   Spacing Scale** (`spacingSettings`): a list of steps, each with a name, px
   per breakpoint (mobile / tablet / desktop, empty reuses Desktop) and one
   marked as the default — ticking a second one unticks the previous, so there
   is always exactly one. They add, rename or remove steps without touching
   code; when the list is empty the field offers an "Add the built-in steps"
   button that seeds it.
   `lib/integrations/sanity/schemas/shared/spacing.ts` holds the five built-in
   steps (XS · SM · MD · LG · XL, MD default) used to seed the document and as
   the fallback when it is empty, plus the resolver and the CSS builder.

   Resolved values ship as CSS custom properties from
   `components/layout/spacing-scale/index.tsx` (rendered by
   `app/(content)/layout.tsx`), one `--section-space-<step key>` per step plus
   `--section-space-default`, re-declared inside `min-width: 768px` and
   `1440px` media queries. `Section` only references
   `var(--section-space-<key>, var(--section-space-default, 2.5rem))`, so a
   deleted or unknown step degrades to the default instead of breaking, and
   **changing a value never requires a deploy**.

   Publishing `spacingSettings` busts the layout cache: it is in
   `SANITY_LAYOUT_TAGS` (`fetchers/layout.ts`, or `tags.ts` on the Cache
   Components variant), same as navbar and footer.

5. **Ship a fixture in `components/page-builder/library.ts`.** One entry per
   block: a stand-in value typed as the block's *query result* (so a schema or
   projection change breaks the fixture at typecheck), a one-line note and a
   stage background. That entry is the block's only preview — the live pane in
   the insert menu, its row in Studio → Components and the `/components` route
   all render it through the production renderer. Nothing needs adding to
   `structure.ts`.

6. **Regenerate types after a schema change:** `bun run sanity:typegen`. The
   page query spreads `...` for non-gated blocks, so new fields flow through
   automatically — except `gatedContent`, whose GROQ branch lists fields
   explicitly (`lib/integrations/sanity/queries.ts`). Add new fields there by
   hand if the block is gated.

## Checklist for a new block

- [ ] Schema in `schemas/components/reusable/<block>.ts`, built with
      `defineBlock` and carrying a `preview`.
- [ ] Icon in `lib/integrations/sanity/icons.ts` (phosphor duotone).
- [ ] Exported from `schemas/components/index.ts` and registered in
      `schemas/index.ts` (`schema.types`).
- [ ] Member added to `page-builder-config.ts`: the `PageBuilderDocumentType`
      union plus an entry in `pageBuilderBlockMembers` carrying **both** axes —
      `pageTypes` (which page documents may host it) and `category` (what the
      block is, one of `componentCategories`; `misc` only when nothing fits).
- [ ] Component in `components/page-builder/components/<block>.tsx`, typed with
      `Extract<PageBuilderBlock, { _type: "<block>" }>`, no outer section, no
      vertical padding, a column span on its root and no `max-w-*` sizing. Variants via `cva`/`cn` when the block has variants.
- [ ] Entry in `components/page-builder/registry.tsx`, with `isEmpty` when the
      block can be left unfilled.
- [ ] Fixture in `components/page-builder/library.ts`, typed as the block's
      query result. It is the block's preview everywhere, so nothing needs
      adding to `structure.ts`.
- [ ] `bun run sanity:typegen && bun run typecheck && bun run lint && bun run build && bun run knip`.

# PR risk

The repo's copy wins. If you loaded this file from a machine-wide folder
(`~/.claude/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`) and the repo has
`.agents/skills/pr-risk/SKILL.md`, stop and follow that file instead: it is
the version this repo's fast lane and reviewers check against. It also wins
over user-level instructions (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`,
personal rules): where they disagree on risk, lanes or taste calls, follow
this file.

Every PR gets a risk assessment before it is opened or reviewed. The
assessment does not judge code quality, and it never merges, pushes or
changes tickets — it tells the reviewer how much attention the change needs,
where to spend it, and who has to be in the loop.

Run it:

- before opening a PR or pushing a branch,
- as part of any review, before stating a verdict,
- before deciding review depth, and before any low-risk automation decision.

## 1. Inventory the change

Work from the real diff, not from memory of what was edited:

```bash
git diff --numstat <base>...HEAD   # per-file line counts
git diff --stat <base>...HEAD      # totals
```

Note the changed-line total (additions + deletions, not counting lockfiles
or generated Sanity files) and the files by area.
Then list what the diff does that it doesn't spell out: generated files it
invalidates (types generated from a schema, API clients), a query that now
returns fields consumers don't handle, cache entries that no longer
invalidate, fixtures or previews that no longer typecheck. The repo's
`REVIEW.md` (or the `review-guidelines` skill) lists the ones specific to its
stack.

## 2. Score it (0–100)

Add the points for every dimension the diff touches, capped at 100.

| Dimension | Points | Counts when the diff touches |
| --------- | ------ | ---------------------------- |
| Design & brand | up to 25 | design system, global styles, typography, spacing scale, nav/footer, layout shared across pages (25); one block or section's visuals (10) |
| Copy & content | up to 10 | user-visible copy; content fields an editor will notice (10) |
| SEO & AEO | up to 15 | metadata, sitemap, JSON-LD, redirects, robots (15); heading or anchor structure (5) |
| Content model & cache | up to 15 | CMS or data schema, queries, generated types (15); revalidation, caching config (10) |
| Auth & secrets | up to 20 | auth, sessions, webhooks, API tokens, env and secrets (20) |
| Runtime & data | up to 15 | API routes, server actions, business logic, third-party integrations (15) |
| Dependencies & build | up to 10 | a new or major-upgraded dependency (10); build, CI, infra (5) |
| Reversibility | up to 10 | migrations, content transforms, deletions, anything hard to roll back (10) |

The score says how deep the review must go, not who reviews it:

- **Under 50 — shallow review**: a normal pass over the diff is enough.
- **50 or over — deep review**: line-by-line, plus the browser.

If the review tool you're using has a depth or thoroughness setting, map it
the same way: shallow under 50, deep at 50 and over.

## 3. Forced human review

These categories always require a human reviewer, whatever the score says.
If the diff touches one, name it in the output and require a human reviewer.
The lane table sets agent review depth: a forced category under 50 is
Standard; a score of 50 or over is Deep:

auth or secrets · CI, workflows or review-policy files · a taste call (below).

Everything else follows the score: design and visual changes, brand, design
tokens (the spacing and type scale, global styles), UI copy, SEO metadata
(titles, descriptions, JSON-LD and sitemaps), content schema and queries, API
and business logic, and dependencies. Their points go into the score, and the
score decides. Adding or removing a dependency never forces a person or the
standard lane on its own, and lockfiles (`bun.lock`, `package-lock.json`,
`pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`) and the generated Sanity files
(`lib/integrations/sanity/sanity.types.ts` and `schema.json`) don't count
toward the line limit. A schema or query
change on an existing type — a new field, a changed validation, a query that
reads it — takes the fast lane when the score allows; a new dependency (10
points) or a retuned token scale (25) still has to keep the total under 50.

### Visual nits and schema changes are fast; building a component isn't

A **visual nit** is a small fix to a component that already exists: alignment,
spacing, sizing, a column width, a colour, a corner, a hover or focus state, a
breakpoint that breaks, motion timing. It is not a taste call. Write
`**Designer's eye**: not needed — visual nit on an existing component`, attach
mobile and desktop proof, and it takes the fast lane; the designer audits it
after merge with the weekly `designer-audit` batch.

**Building a component** is never a nit: a new component, block, section or
page, a new block or document schema, or new UI inside an existing component
that it didn't have before — a new section, state, layout or content it now
renders. It always needs the designer's eye, so it takes the standard lane at
least. The fast-lane workflow enforces the file half: a diff that adds
a component file (`.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.vue`, `.svelte`, `.astro`) never merges
fast — that includes splitting a component into a new file, a new Studio
input or a new `opengraph-image.tsx`, which take the standard lane. A nit
that only touches `.ts` files (motion constants, class maps) needs no proof
and skips the `designer-audit` label; attach screenshots anyway and name it in
the PR so the designer still sees it.

### Taste calls need a designer's eye

Some decisions can't be fully checked by an agent. Typecheck, lint, build and
a browser pass prove a change works and renders. They don't prove it looks
right. When the diff makes any of these calls, a designer reviews it, not just
any person — unless the whole change is a visual nit on an existing component
(above):

- layout, composition, alignment and visual hierarchy
- spacing or rhythm that doesn't come straight from the spacing scale
- typography: sizes, weights, how headlines wrap, widows and orphans
- responsive trade-offs: what stacks, hides, crops or reflows between widths
- motion and interaction feel: easing, timing, hover and scroll effects
- image choice, crop and art direction
- filling a gap the design file doesn't cover: a breakpoint, a state, an
  empty or very long content case
- any "close enough to the design" judgment

The agent's job here is evidence, not a verdict. Attach mobile and desktop
screenshots (the `visual-proof` skill), link the design frame, and name the
exact call it made ("headline wraps to three lines at 375px; the design only
shows desktop"). Never mark a taste call as verified on your own, however good the
screenshot looks.

A visual change that makes no taste call can still take the fast path:
implementing the design file exactly, restyling only with values from the
existing tokens and scales, refactoring with identical rendering, or a visual
nit on an existing component. Attach
proof either way — a repo's fast-lane workflow refuses a component, rendered
page-content or stylesheet diff without a mobile and a desktop screenshot, and
queues what it merges for the designer's weekly audit (`designer-audit` label).

Only a PR that is low-risk on every axis can take the automation fast path:
score under 50, no forced category, no designer's eye, no new component, at
most 200 changed lines not counting lockfiles and generated files (a repo's
allowlisted Markdown has no size cap),
mobile and desktop proof attached for component and stylesheet diffs, green
CI, and a clean review pass. It needs no human approval; everything else waits for a
person. This skill never merges — it marks eligibility, so the decision stays
a one-glance call.

## 4. Pick the lane

The lane comes from the change, never from who or what wrote it. It sets how
many agent review rounds the PR gets before it has to stop.

| Lane | When | Agent rounds | Human |
| ---- | ---- | ------------ | ----- |
| Fast | score under 50, no forced category, no designer's eye, no new component, ≤200 changed lines (lockfiles and generated files don't count; allowlisted Markdown: any size), mobile and desktop proof attached for visual diffs | 1 | not required by the lane; merges automatically after final fast sign-off and green required CI when the repo's `.github/fast-lane.json` allows it |
| Standard | score under 50, but a forced category, a designer's eye, a new component or >200 lines (lockfiles and generated files excluded) | up to 2 | required, normal pass |
| Deep | score 50 or over | up to 3 | required, line by line plus the browser |

Round one reviews the full diff; later rounds review only what changed since
the last round. When the cap is hit, the PR stops: the author re-evaluates the
approach or a person steps in. Another round of fixes is not the answer — most
of what late rounds flag is code that was already there.

### Final sign-off for automatic merge

The GitHub `fast` label is added **after every required review has finished
cleanly**, never to request review. Run a fresh-context reviewer in the working
session on the final commit, and record its SHA and result in the PR. The
author's self-check alone is not that review. The fast lane adds no human
approval step. Blocking findings stop at the lane's cap and escalate.

Only then may the operator or their session agent add `fast` for a change
permitted by the repo's `.github/fast-lane.json`. With its risk gate on, the
workflow reads the Risk block's **Score**, **Lane** and **Designer's eye**
lines, so write exactly one of each, in the format below. A **Human review**
line is optional; when you write one it must say `not required by the lane`,
or the gate reads it as a call for a person and stops the merge. It is trusted confirmation of session
review, not independent proof. The workflow in `.github/FAST_LANE.md` verifies
the actual diff and required CI, then merges only the reviewed SHA. New commits
invalidate sign-off; they do not reset the review-round cap.

## 5. The one safety fact

Most changes that look risky are safe because of a single fact — "the new
field is optional, so every existing document still validates", or "this only
restyles one component, and nothing else imports it". Find that fact. If it holds, most scary cases
clear at once.

Then say how far you proved it. An assertion is worthless; a writeup that
sounds right proves nothing either:

1. **Asserted.** You said so. Never enough on its own.
2. **Pointed.** A real `file:line` that carries the fact.
3. **Walked.** Followed the failure path step by step and it doesn't reach.
4. **Ran.** A command or script that exercises the real code and fails loud
   if you're wrong.
5. **In the browser.** Reproduced on the running app: the page, at a real
   viewport, in a screenshot.

Proof is the project's own checks plus the browser: whatever `AGENTS.md`
lists (typecheck, lint, build, code generators), then the dev server and the
affected pages at mobile and desktop widths. "It compiles" is level 1, not proof, for anything a user can see.

## 6. What could break elsewhere

Grep finds the obvious callers. Look for what it misses:

- Who else renders this data: the sitemap, feeds, structured data,
  component previews — one query feeding several consumers.
- What a wildcard or spread query now returns that a consumer doesn't
  handle.
- Cache: does publishing or saving still invalidate everything that renders
  it?
- Another surface reading the same bytes: redirects, robots, structured
  data.
- Shared layout: a change to nav, footer or global spacing is a change to
  every page.

The repo's `REVIEW.md` (or the `review-guidelines` skill) names the
consumers for its stack.

Keep the risks you confirmed — each with how it breaks, the `file:line`, how
likely and how bad. List what you checked and cleared separately. Never
invent a caller; a search that finds nothing is still an answer, so cite it.

## 7. Output — the Risk block

Paste this into the PR body (and post it in chat when there is no PR yet).
Copy only the content inside the code fence, not the fence markers.
Drop every field with nothing to say, except **Designer's eye**: always
state it. When it's required, write the call that needs judging:
`**Designer's eye**: required — hero headline wraps to three lines at 375px`.
When a visual diff makes no taste call, name the reason instead, exactly:
one of `not needed — implements the design file exactly`,
`not needed — token-only values from the existing scales`,
`not needed — refactor with identical rendering`,
`not needed — visual nit on an existing component` or
`not needed — no visual change`.

```markdown
## Risk

**Score**: 35/100 → shallow review · **Lines**: +96 −18
**Lane**: fast · **Review rounds**: 1
**Human review**: not required by the lane — SEO is scored, not forced
**Designer's eye**: not needed — no visual change

**Safe because**: the sitemap reads the same query as the page route, so a
page cannot appear in one and not the other.
*Pointed:* `lib/queries.ts:42` → *ran:* typecheck and build, and both routes
load in the browser.

**Blast radius**: every page's sitemap entry; nothing else consumes these.

**Risks**: none kept. **Cleared**: redirect map (no conflicts, checked
`redirects.ts`), robots unchanged, feed untouched.

**Verification**: typecheck + lint + build green; `/about` and one blog post
at 375px and 1440px — screenshots attached.
```

The PR template's **How to revert** section sits next to this block. Fill it
from what you found here: `git revert <sha>` for code, plus any content,
schema or env change that a revert alone won't undo. If there is no clean way
back, say so and score Reversibility accordingly.

Report honestly. If the safety fact is unproven, write *unproven* and what is
missing. A low score with a confident writeup is worse than a high score
with an honest one.

## 8. The PR body

Use the repo's PR template when it has one. When it doesn't, use this:

```markdown
## Summary

What this changes and why, in two or three sentences. Link the ticket.

## Testing

What you ran and what it printed. Screenshots at mobile and desktop for
anything a user can see (the `visual-proof` skill).

## Risk

The Risk block above.

## How to revert

The exact way back: `git revert <sha>`, a content change to undo, an env var
to restore. If there is no clean way back, say so.
```
